market_definition.category: Inventory planning and demand forecasting software sold to independent pharmacy operators in North America — a workflow layer sitting between the pharmacy's dispensing system and the wholesaler's ordering system. The provided material characterises the competitive substitute for this function as the reordering tools the three national pharmaceutical wholesalers supply to their customers at no charge as part of the distribution agreement [S4].
market_definition.boundary_notes: The material supports drawing the boundary at 'the reordering decision for an independent pharmacy group', because that is the function the free wholesaler tools already perform [S4]. Two boundaries matter and the research does not resolve either. First, whether forecasting is a separable product or a feature of an ordering workflow that is already bundled into a distribution agreement — S4 establishes that the ordering workflow is bundled and free, but says nothing about whether forecasting specifically is. Second, whether the buyer is the group (multi-store operator) or the store; S3 counts groups, not stores, so the entire addressable unit count in the material is expressed in groups and cannot be converted to stores or to dollars from anything provided. The material contains no dollar-denominated sizing of this category at all — no TAM, SAM, ACV, or price point comes from any source given to me. The deck's own figures (C7-C9, C13) are deck claims, not research, and are outside my remit here.
how_analysts_segment_it: By buyer scale — S4 segments explicitly on this axis, noting that the zero price of the wholesaler tool 'makes them the default option for smaller groups', which implies larger groups are the segment where a paid alternative is even considered [S4].

By cohort position relative to first renewal — S1 and S2 both segment the customer base at the first renewal boundary, S1 for retention measurement and S2 for churn concentration [S1][S2]. This is a segmentation of customers, not of the market, but it is the only segmentation the material actually performs on this category.

By implementation risk at the data-migration step — S2 identifies migration from the wholesaler's ordering system as the point where failed implementations fail, which functionally splits prospects into those whose wholesaler data can be migrated and those whose cannot [S2].

Inference, not read from a source: the material does not contain any analyst-house segmentation of this category. No source given to me names a research firm, a market map, or a category taxonomy. I could not verify how, or whether, analysts segment this market at all.

tam_estimates.value: approximately 21,000-23,000 independent pharmacy groups in North America (a unit count of potential buyers, NOT a dollar TAM — no source provided to me converts this to revenue)
tam_estimates.year: 2026-03 (date of the source; the source does not state the year the count refers to)
tam_estimates.source: S3, 'Independent pharmacy groups in North America' — an unattributed research summary with no named publisher
tam_estimates.methodology: Not stated. S3 gives the count and its trend but does not describe how the count was constructed, what qualifies a 'group', or whether it counts groups or stores.

sizing.consensus_view: There is no consensus view to report, because there is no dollar sizing in the material to form one from. The only quantified boundary on this market anywhere in the four sources is a headcount of buyers: 21,000-23,000 independent pharmacy groups in North America, declining 3-4% annually for six years as groups are acquired by regional chains [S3]. That decline is the most important sizing fact available: the unit base of this market has been shrinking for six consecutive years, and the mechanism of the shrinkage — absorption into regional chains [S3] — removes buyers from the independent segment specifically, which is the segment this category serves. A market that loses 3-4% of its addressable accounts per year needs share gains of roughly that magnitude just to hold revenue flat, before any growth. I am inferring the compounding implication; S3 states only the annual rate and the six-year duration, not a cumulative figure, and I will not compute one and present it as sourced.
sizing.cagr_range: Unit count: -3% to -4% annually, sustained over six years [S3]. Revenue CAGR: unknown — no source provided to me states a revenue growth rate for this category, and unit decline cannot be converted to revenue growth without a price trend, which is also absent.
sizing.why_estimates_diverge: There are no competing estimates to diverge, which is itself the finding. Exactly one source addresses market size and it reports a single internally-consistent range (21,000-23,000) whose 10% width is not explained by the source [S3]. With no second independent count, I cannot tell whether that width reflects genuine measurement uncertainty, definitional disagreement about what constitutes a 'group' versus a store or a banner, or the six-year decline being measured at different points. The absence of any dollar-denominated third-party sizing means every revenue-scale claim about this market in the deck rests on the deck's own arithmetic rather than on anything I was given to check it against.

tailwinds: A real and specific quality gap in the incumbent free tooling: independent analyses cited by S4 describe the wholesalers' reorder tools as optimising for wholesaler fill rates rather than for pharmacy margin [S4]. This is a structural misalignment of interest, not a temporary product deficiency — the party supplying the tool is the party on the other side of the transaction it optimises. Misalignment of that kind does not get fixed by the incumbent improving its software, which is what makes it a durable opening.

The buying unit is a group rather than a single store [S3], which in principle allows a vendor to grow inside an account as the group adds stores. I note this as a structural feature of the buyer, not as evidence that expansion actually occurs — no source provided to me measures expansion revenue in this category.
headwinds: The addressable base is contracting: -3% to -4% per year for six years, via acquisition of independent groups by regional chains [S3]. Each acquisition removes a prospect, and plausibly removes a customer, since the acquiring regional chain is not an independent group and may run its own systems. The material does not confirm what happens to a customer's contract when its group is acquired — that is a gap, and a material one, because it determines whether this decline is a slow drain on the prospect pool or an active source of churn.

A free, pre-installed, contractually-bundled substitute exists at every prospect: all three national wholesalers supply reorder tooling at no charge as part of the distribution agreement, and zero price makes them the default for smaller groups [S4]. The paid product is therefore never competing against 'nothing' — it is competing against 'already installed, already paid for, already the default'.

Severe first-year attrition: 30-35% first-year logo churn in software sold to independent pharmacy operators, concentrated before the first renewal [S2]. Roughly a third of everything sold into this market does not survive its first year. This is a property of the market, not of any one vendor.

The failure mode is technical and sits at the hardest possible point: failed implementations typically fail during the initial data migration from the wholesaler's ordering system [S2]. The vendor whose product must displace the wholesaler tool must first successfully extract data from it, and that dependency is where a third of deals die.
demand_signals.buyer_budget_reality: No source provided to me states a budget, a price point, a willingness-to-pay figure, or an ACV benchmark for this category. What the material does establish is the shape of the budget conversation rather than its size: the buyer's current spend on this function is zero, because the wholesaler supplies the tool as part of a distribution agreement already in place [S4]. Any purchase here is net-new budget creation, not budget displacement — the vendor is not taking a line item from an incumbent, it is asking a small operator to create one. S4's observation that zero price makes the wholesaler tool the default 'for smaller groups' specifically implies price sensitivity varies sharply by group size, and that the viable paid segment is the larger end of the 21,000-23,000 groups [S3][S4] — but no source I was given quantifies that split, so I cannot say what fraction of the base is actually addressable at any price.

incumbents.name: The three national pharmaceutical wholesalers (individual companies are NOT named in any source provided to me; S4 refers to them only as 'the three national pharmaceutical wholesalers')
incumbents.position: The default incumbent at essentially every prospect. Each supplies inventory reordering tools to its customers at no charge as part of the distribution agreement [S4]. Distribution is where the relationship already lives, so the tool arrives with the contract rather than being sold. Independent analyses cited in S4 describe these tools as optimising for wholesaler fill rates rather than pharmacy margin, which is a genuine weakness — but S4 pairs that criticism directly with the observation that zero price makes them the default option for smaller groups [S4]. Both halves of that sentence matter: the tools are worse AND they win by default.
incumbents.funding_or_scale: Not stated in any source provided to me. S4 establishes only that there are three, that they are national, and that the tooling is bundled into distribution agreements.

incumbents.name: Regional pharmacy chains (as acquirers of the buyer base, not as software competitors)
incumbents.position: Not a competitor in the product sense, but they are the mechanism removing 3-4% of the addressable base annually and have been for six years [S3]. A group that is acquired by a regional chain stops being an independent group. Whether it also stops being a customer is not established by any source I was given. I include them here because in a market defined by buyer count, the entity consuming the buyer count is a competitive fact.
incumbents.funding_or_scale: Not stated in any source provided to me.

adjacent_threats: Pharmacy management and dispensing systems: the material establishes that dispensing history exists as a data source distinct from purchase history (this is the axis the deck's C12 claims to compete on), and S2 establishes that the wholesaler's ordering system holds the migratable data [S2]. Whoever owns the dispensing system sits on the input that makes dispensing-reconciled forecasting possible. No source provided to me names any dispensing-system vendor, states whether any offers forecasting, or describes their posture toward this category — so I flag the adjacency as structurally obvious and evidentially unverified.

The wholesalers themselves moving up-market from reorder tooling into margin-aware forecasting. S4 gives no evidence that they intend to, and the fill-rate incentive S4 describes arguably cuts against it. But they already own the distribution relationship, the ordering workflow, the purchase-history data and a zero-price channel [S4] — four of the things a competitor would otherwise have to build.

Group purchasing organisations, buying groups, and franchise/banner programs for independents: a natural aggregator of exactly this buyer. Not mentioned in any source provided to me — listed as an unverified structural adjacency, not a finding.
differentiation_axes: Whose margin the tool optimises for — the pharmacy's or the wholesaler's. S4 makes this the explicit axis on which the incumbent tooling is criticised [S4], and it is the only axis of product differentiation any source provided to me actually identifies.

Ability to complete the initial data migration out of the wholesaler's ordering system — S2 identifies this as where implementations fail [S2], which makes migration competence a competitive capability rather than a delivery detail.
Surviving the first renewal at all, given 30-35% first-year logo churn in this buyer segment [S2].

saturation.consolidation_activity: None seen at the software-vendor level — no source provided to me records any acquisition, merger, or shutdown of a software company in this category. The only consolidation the material documents is at the CUSTOMER level: independent pharmacy groups being acquired by regional chains at 3-4% per year for six years [S3]. That is buyer-side consolidation, which affects this market's size but is not evidence about vendor-side saturation.
saturation.why: I want to be precise about how weak this read is. I found ZERO funded competitors — not because I established that none exist, but because none of the four sources I was given names a single software vendor in this category, funded or otherwise. `funded_competitors_known` is null rather than 0 for exactly that reason: absence of evidence in a four-source bibliography is not evidence of absence, and reporting '0 funded competitors' would dress up a research gap as a market finding. With no vendor names, no round announcements and no dates, I cannot observe entry flow, so `new_entrants_trend` is unknown; with no price points from any source, I cannot observe compression, so `pricing_direction` is unknown. What I CAN say rests on evidence. The niche that remains is defined by S4's two-part finding: the incumbent tooling is free and default, but is described by independent analyses as optimising for the wholesaler rather than the pharmacy [S4]. That misalignment is structural — it follows from who supplies the tool — so it will not close on its own, and it defines a real wedge. The niche is narrow rather than wide-open for three reasons the material does support: the buyer base is shrinking 3-4% annually [S3], a third of first-year customers churn out before renewal [S2], and every prospect already has a zero-cost tool installed [S4]. 'Emerging' as lifecycle stage is likewise an inference from the absence of any documented vendor activity — no funding, no acquisitions, no named players — rather than a positive observation of an early market, and it should be read as low-confidence.

likely_absorbers.name: The three national pharmaceutical wholesalers (not individually named in any source provided to me)
likely_absorbers.why_them: They already own every input this product needs and every channel it would use. The distribution agreement is already signed with the customer; the ordering workflow already runs on their system; the purchase history already sits in their database [S4]; and S2 confirms the migration path out of their ordering system is the hard technical step for anyone else [S2]. A vendor entering this category must extract data from the incumbent's system to displace the incumbent's tool — that is an unusually adverse structural position.
signals_already_visible: This is not a future risk — the bundle already exists and already ships. All three national wholesalers supply inventory reordering tools at no charge as part of the distribution agreement [S4]. The absorption pattern the question asks about has already run for the base reordering function; the only live question is whether it extends to margin-aware, dispensing-reconciled forecasting.
Zero price has already made the bundled tool the default option for smaller groups [S4] — i.e. the bundle is not merely present but is winning by default in at least one named segment.

No source provided to me shows any wholesaler shipping, hiring for, or announcing a dispensing-reconciled or margin-optimising forecasting capability. There is no roadmap statement, job posting or acquisition in the material. That absence is why my verdict is 'contested' rather than 'feature'.

precedents.why_it_is_comparable: I am deliberately citing no precedent. The prompt's examples (antivirus, file sync, VPN, screen sharing, password management) all describe a platform absorbing a category AFTER startups proved it out. The mechanism here does not match that shape: the bundling came first, the free tool is the incumbent, and a paid entrant is attempting to displace it. Invoking a consumer-platform precedent would import a story the evidence does not support, and no source provided to me contains any precedent case at all.

what_would_prevent_it: The incentive misalignment is structural and self-reinforcing. A wholesaler-supplied tool that genuinely optimised for pharmacy margin would work against the wholesaler's own fill rates — the interest S4 says the current tools serve [S4]. This is the single strongest reason the category can stay standalone: the absorber has a positive reason not to build the differentiated version, not merely an absence of interest.

Data access on the dispensing side. If reconciliation against dispensing history (rather than purchase history) requires data the wholesaler does not hold, the wholesaler cannot trivially replicate it. The material establishes that the wholesaler holds the ORDERING data [S2][S4]; no source provided to me states who holds dispensing data or on what terms it can be accessed. This is the pivotal unverified question in the whole analysis and I flag it as such rather than assuming either answer.

Workflow depth and switching cost after a successful implementation. S2 establishes that migration is hard enough to kill a third of first-year deals [S2]; the same difficulty, once survived, is a wall against the next vendor. I am inferring the reverse-direction implication — S2 states the failure rate, not the retention benefit.

A buyer who will not consolidate: independent groups are, by definition, operators who have not sold to a chain. But S3 shows this cohort is being consolidated at 3-4% per year regardless [S3], so this is the weakest of the four protections.
absorption_risk.notes: The honest framing is that this category has ALREADY been absorbed once, at the basic-reordering level, and the entrant's thesis is that the absorbed version is bad in a specific and structurally durable way [S4]. That is a materially different risk profile from a category awaiting absorption. The upside case is that the absorber's own economics prevent it from closing the gap; the downside case is that the absorber does not have to close the gap, because free and adequate beats paid and better for the smaller groups that make up an unquantified but evidently large share of the 21,000-23,000 base [S3][S4]. I set confidence to medium rather than high because the decisive fact — whether dispensing-history data is accessible to the wholesalers — is not in any source I was given.

open_source_landscape.evidence_for_the_gap: No assessment is possible and none is offered. Not one of the four sources provided to me mentions an open-source project, repository, library, foundation, or community effort in pharmacy inventory planning or demand forecasting. Rather than construct a plausible-sounding OSS landscape from general knowledge — which would mean citing no source and asserting adoption evidence I have not seen — I am setting applicable to false and recording the absence as a research gap.
open_source_landscape.notes: One qualification on `applicable: false`, and it matters. The OSS mechanism the prompt describes — a free alternative reaching parity, capability stopping being the differentiator, and the residual competition shifting to packaging, operations, support and distribution, which a platform vendor already owns — is playing out in this market in full, just not via open source. The free alternative is the wholesaler's bundled reorder tool [S4]. The 'platform vendor that already owns distribution' is the wholesaler, who literally owns physical distribution to the customer [S4]. The price floor a credible free alternative imposes is already in place, which is why I set pricing_pressure to 'significant' despite there being no OSS: S4 states plainly that zero price makes the incumbent tool the default for smaller groups [S4], and that caps what anyone can charge them. The one part of the mechanism NOT satisfied is parity — S4 reports independent analyses describing the free tools as optimising for the wholesaler rather than the pharmacy [S4], i.e. the free option is meaningfully behind on the axis that matters to the buyer. By the prompt's own framework that is the healthy configuration: customers can still be asked to pay for something they cannot get free. The question is whether the residual gap is the Kubernetes/Docker kind (distribution — which the wholesaler owns outright, and which would be fatal) or the Snowflake kind (genuinely hard to give away — which the misaligned-incentive argument suggests). On the evidence I was given it is closer to the Snowflake case, because the incumbent has a reason not to close the gap, but the distribution disadvantage is severe and real. Separately: I am NOT assessing 'pricing_direction' in the saturation block as compressing on this basis — a free floor that has existed all along is a structural cap, not evidence of a downward trend, and no source I was given contains a price series.

adjacent_markets.market: Pharmacy dispensing / pharmacy management systems (the system of record for dispensing history)
adjacent_markets.why_it_matters: This is the upstream data source for any forecast reconciled against dispensing rather than purchase history. Whoever controls that system controls the input. No source provided to me names a vendor in this market, states its structure, or describes data-access terms — so I can identify the dependency but not evaluate it. Given that the entire product differentiation in this category (per S4's critique of purchase-history-driven wholesaler tools [S4]) turns on having better demand signal, an unverified dependency on an unnamed upstream system-of-record is the most important thing I could not check.

adjacent_markets.size_note: Not stated in any source provided to me beyond the fact that there are three national wholesalers [S4].
adjacent_markets.why_it_matters: Convergence has already occurred from the distribution side: wholesalers supply the software as a term of the distribution agreement [S4], which means the software market and the distribution market are not separable at the point of sale. A vendor here is not entering a software market that happens to sit near distribution; it is entering a distribution relationship that already includes software.

adjacent_markets.size_note: Absorbing 3-4% of the independent group base annually, sustained over six years [S3].
adjacent_markets.why_it_matters: Acquisition by a regional chain is a substitute solution to the operator's problem — the operator stops making its own inventory decisions. Every year this substitute takes 3-4% of the buyer base off the table [S3]. Whether the acquiring chain retains, replaces or expands the software contract is not addressed by any source provided to me, and determines whether chain consolidation is an expansion channel or a churn channel.

economics.typical_pricing: Not stated in any source provided to me. The only price fact in the entire bibliography is the incumbent's: zero, bundled into the distribution agreement [S4]. No source gives an ACV, list price, per-store rate, or contract benchmark for a paid product in this category. The deck's $62k ACV (C9) is a deck claim with no corroborating source in this bibliography, and I make no assessment of it here.
economics.typical_gross_margin: Not stated in any source provided to me. No margin data for this category appears in the material. I decline to substitute a generic SaaS margin figure, since the implementation burden S2 documents — migrations hard enough to kill 30-35% of first-year customers [S2] — is exactly the kind of cost that makes generic SaaS margin assumptions wrong in vertical categories, and I have no data to size it.
economics.typical_cac_payback: Not stated in any source provided to me. It can, however, be bounded qualitatively and unfavourably: with 30-35% of logos churning in the first year, concentrated before the first renewal [S2], roughly a third of all acquisition cost in this market never reaches a renewal at all. Whatever the nominal payback period on a surviving customer, the blended figure across a cohort is materially worse. That is an inference from S2's churn figure, not a payback number from any source.

funding_environment.valuation_norms: Not stated in any source provided to me. The bibliography contains no funding round, no valuation, no multiple and no investor for this category or any company in it. I cannot assess whether the deck's raise terms (C13) are in line with norms, because I was given no norms.
exit_comps: None available. No source provided to me records an acquisition, IPO, or exit of any software company in pharmacy inventory planning or adjacent vertical SaaS.
funding_environment.notes: Setting investor_appetite is close to guesswork here and I want that on the record: it is the schema's only non-null option set and no source I was given contains a single data point about capital flowing into this category. 'Steady' should be read as 'no signal', not as an observation. The one funding-adjacent fact in the material is S1's existence — retention benchmarks for vertical SaaS are published at all [S1], which implies an investor audience that tracks the sector — but that is thin evidence about appetite and I would not build anything on it. Note also, on the definitional point S1 raises: vertical SaaS retention benchmarks are published on an all-customer basis at 104-112%, and a cohort restricted to customers past their first renewal typically reports 25-40 points higher for the same business, because the customers most likely to churn have already been excluded from the denominator — so the two bases are not comparable [S1]. This is a market-structure fact about how the category's benchmarks are constructed. Applying it to any particular company's claims is the comparison agent's job, not mine, and I have not done it here.

factors: Structural, not regulatory, and the dominant fact in this market: software in this category is supplied as a term of a commercial distribution agreement rather than sold on its own merits [S4]. That contractual bundling is the single largest barrier to entry described anywhere in the material, and it is not a regulatory barrier — it is a private-contract one, which means no regulator will remove it.

Structural incentive misalignment in the incumbent tooling: independent analyses describe the wholesalers' tools as optimising for wholesaler fill rates rather than pharmacy margin [S4]. Durable, because it follows from who pays for the tool.
Ongoing consolidation of the buyer base: independent groups acquired by regional chains at 3-4% annually for six years [S3].

Data portability at the migration boundary: implementations fail during initial data migration from the wholesaler's ordering system [S2]. The material does not say whether this reflects technical complexity, data-format opacity, contractual restriction, or active resistance by the wholesaler — and the difference matters enormously for whether the barrier can be engineered away. Unverified.

Not addressed in any source provided to me: pharmacy licensing, controlled-substance handling and reporting, DSCSA/track-and-trace or equivalent supply-chain regulation, PHI/privacy obligations attaching to dispensing data, or state-level pharmacy board requirements. Any of these could bear materially on a product that touches dispensing history, and none of them appears in the bibliography. My 'medium' risk level is set on what I could see; the unexamined regulatory surface here is large and PHI exposure in particular could move it.

sources.title: How retention is measured in vertical SaaS, and why the figures diverge
sources.what_it_supported: All-customer NRR in vertical SaaS benchmarks at 104-112%; a cohort restricted to customers past their first renewal typically reports 25-40 points higher than the all-customer figure for the same business, because the customers most likely to churn have already been excluded from the denominator; benchmarks are published on the all-customer basis, so the two are not comparable. Reliability marked unknown, not secondary: the source has no named publisher, no stated methodology, no sample size and no panel definition, and its domain (research.example.org) does not identify a real research organisation. Under the reliability ranking I hold myself to, an unattributed summary ranks below an analyst-house release. The definitional point it makes is internally coherent and mechanically sound on its face, which is why I use it — but I cannot verify the 104-112% or 25-40-point figures against anything.

sources.title: First-year attrition in pharmacy operations software
sources.what_it_supported: First-year logo churn of 30-35% in software sold to independent pharmacy operators, concentrated before the first renewal; failed implementations typically fail during initial data migration from the wholesaler's ordering system. Supported my headwinds, differentiation axes, CAC-payback commentary and the workflow-depth argument in absorption. Same attribution problem as S1 — no publisher, no methodology, no sample.

sources.title: Independent pharmacy groups in North America
sources.what_it_supported: Approximately 21,000-23,000 independent pharmacy groups in North America; count has declined 3-4% annually for six years as groups are acquired by regional chains. The sole sizing input in this analysis, and the basis for the negative unit CAGR and the buyer-consolidation adjacency. No publisher, no methodology, no definition of 'group', and no explanation of the 10% range width.

sources.title: Wholesaler reorder tooling
sources.what_it_supported: The three national pharmaceutical wholesalers each supply inventory reordering tools to their customers at no charge as part of the distribution agreement; independent analyses describe these tools as optimising for wholesaler fill rates rather than pharmacy margin, but note that their zero price makes them the default option for smaller groups. The single most load-bearing source in this analysis — it supplies the incumbent, the pricing floor, the absorption mechanism and the differentiation axis. Note that S4 reports its central criticism at second hand ('independent analyses describe...') without naming those analyses, so the fill-rate claim is hearsay within an unattributed summary and is weighted accordingly. Its zero-price and bundling claims are structural and more readily credible than its evaluative claims.

research_gaps: No competitor is named anywhere in the bibliography. Not one software vendor in this category — incumbent, challenger, funded or bootstrapped — appears by name in any of the four sources. Even the three wholesalers are referred to only by role [S4]. A competitive landscape with no named competitors is the largest gap in this analysis and it caps the confidence of everything in that section.

No dollar sizing of any kind. No TAM, SAM, ACV, price point, revenue figure or growth rate for this category appears in any source. The only quantity available is a headcount of buyers [S3]. Every revenue-scale statement about this market therefore rests on arithmetic no source I was given can check.

No funding data. No round, valuation, multiple, investor or exit for this category or any adjacent one. The funding_environment section is essentially empty as a result, and investor_appetite is unsupported.
No open-source evidence in either direction. I could not confirm that OSS forecasting projects relevant to this category exist, nor that they do not.

Whether the deck's claimed differentiator is technically achievable: no source provided to me establishes who holds dispensing history, whether it is accessible to a third-party vendor, or on what commercial or legal terms. This is the pivotal question for both the differentiation thesis and the absorption risk, and I could verify nothing about it.

What happens to a customer contract when its group is acquired by a regional chain. S3 documents the 3-4% annual attrition of independent groups [S3] but not its effect on installed software, which determines whether buyer consolidation is a churn channel or an expansion channel.
Whether the migration difficulty S2 identifies [S2] is technical, contractual, or the result of active resistance by the wholesaler. The remedies differ completely.

No regulatory sources at all: nothing on DSCSA/track-and-trace, PHI/privacy obligations on dispensing data, state pharmacy board requirements, or controlled-substance reporting. My medium risk rating covers only the structural factors I could see.

Provenance of the entire bibliography. All four sources sit on the same placeholder domain (research.example.org), carry the same date (2026-03), were all surfaced by the same query ('vertical SaaS net revenue retention benchmark'), and none names a publisher, author, methodology or sample. They may share a single upstream origin, in which case the apparent corroboration across four sources is illusory — they would be one voice, not four. I have rated all four 'unknown' on reliability for this reason and set sizing_confidence to low. Notably, S3 and S4 — the pharmacy-market sources — were retrieved by a query about SaaS retention benchmarks, which suggests the research sweep was organised around the deck's retention claims rather than around the market itself, and that the market-side coverage is incidental rather than systematic.
